Rendered Depth-Guided Warping is a consistency regularization technique used during NeRF training to enforce geometric coherence between observed and unobserved viewpoints without the computational cost of full-resolution rendering [S1, unofficial].

It confirms that this is done using low-resolution patches (stride s=2) upsampled via bilinear interpolation to avoid the computational cost of full-resolution rendering, which aligns perfectly with the claim.

It generates a warped image from a source view using a low-resolution rendered depth map from a target view, enabling the computation of a consistency loss that encourages globally consistent geometry and appearance [S1, unofficial].

The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly describes a method where rays are sampled on a strided grid (stride s=2) to create low-resolution patches, which are then used to render a depth map ($D_j$). This low-resolution depth map is upsampled to full resolution for inverse warping to generate a warped image ($I_{i->j}$) from a source view ($I_i$). The text further states that a consistency loss ($L_{cons}$) is applied between the unobserved viewpoint image and the warped observed viewpoint image to encourage globally consistent rendering.
supported

Rendering a full image can take tens of seconds per iteration; strided sampling with $s=2$ reduces this cost to a fraction, enabling efficient consistency regularization during training [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that rendering a full image takes tens of seconds per iteration and that strided sampling with s=2 reduces this cost. The provided text from Source [S1] explicitly confirms both points: under the 'Acceleration' section, it states, 'Rendering a full image is computationally heavy and extremely timetaking, requiring tens of seconds for a single iteration.' It immediately follows with, 'rays are sampled on a strided grid to make the patch with stride s, which we have set as 2.' It further explains that this method allows generating detailed warped patches 'with only a fraction of computational cost that would be required when rendering the original sized ray batch.'

The claim states that for each sampled ray, the NeRF model is queried for density σ and integrated to render a depth value. The claim accurately reflects the methodology described in the text.
